passages.happening:
David confers with his leaders and says to the whole assembly that, if it seems good and is of the LORD, they should send word to all their brothers and to the priests and Levites, ‘Then let us bring back the ark of our God, for we did not inquire of Him in the days of Saul’ (verse 3). ‘And because this proposal seemed right to all the people, the whole assembly agreed to it’ (verse 4).

David gathers all Israel, ‘from the River Shihor in Egypt to Lebo-hamath’ (verse 5), and they go to Kiriath-jearim to bring up ‘the ark of God the LORD, who is enthroned between the cherubim’ (verse 6). They carry it from Abinadab's house on a new cart, with Uzzah and Ahio guiding it (verse 7). ‘David and all the Israelites were celebrating before God with all their might, with songs and on harps and lyres, with tambourines, cymbals, and trumpets’ (verse 8).
passages.hearers:
David's first great act as king, in the Chronicler's telling, is not a war but a return to God's worship. It fits the book's picture of David as the founder of Israel's worship. The account follows 2 Samuel 6, with an added introduction in which David consults the leaders and the assembly. Chronicles places it right after the capture of Jerusalem, where 2 Samuel puts other events first; the Chronicler seems to have arranged his material by theme, to show the ark as David's first concern.

The ark was a wooden chest overlaid with gold, holding the tablets of the covenant, with two golden cherubim facing each other on its cover. It was understood as the footstool of God's throne, the place where the LORD was especially present among his people, the holiest object in Israel. It had been at Kiriath-jearim, about eight or nine miles west of Jerusalem, since the Philistines sent it back. In Saul's days it was not sought; the verb is darash, the word on which Saul was judged in chapter 10.

The boundaries in verse 5, from Egypt's border to the far north, describe the full extent of the land promised to Israel.
passages.later: First Samuel says that ‘a long time passed, twenty years in all, as the ark remained at Kiriath-jearim’ (1 Samuel 7:2).
passages.asks: David consulted everyone, and everyone agreed, and the joy was real. Ask whether something can be zealous, joyful and agreed by all, and still not be done God's way. And ask what you have assumed God wants without asking him.

passages.t: Uzzah, and the house of Obed-edom
passages.happening:
‘When they came to the threshing floor of Chidon, Uzzah reached out and took hold of the ark, because the oxen had stumbled’ (verse 9). ‘And the anger of the LORD burned against Uzzah, and He struck him down because he had put his hand on the ark. So he died there before God’ (verse 10).

‘Then David became angry because the LORD had burst forth against Uzzah; so he named that place Perez-uzzah’ (verse 11). ‘That day David feared God’ (verse 12), and asked how he could ever bring the ark to himself. He leaves it at the house of Obed-edom the Gittite, where it stays three months, ‘and the LORD blessed his household and everything he owned’ (verse 14).
passages.hearers:
The law said exactly how the ark was to be moved. Levites of the clan of Kohath were to carry it on their shoulders with poles, after the priests had covered it, and they were not to touch the holy things, or they would die. A new cart was a respectable way to move a precious object, and it was how the Philistines had sent the ark back. But it was their method, not God's.

A play on words ties the chapter together. David proposed to send word far and wide, literally to break out, parats; the LORD broke out, parats, against Uzzah, and the place was named the breaking out against Uzzah. The same phrase marks both the joy and the death: they celebrated before God, and he died there before God.

The ark that brought death to Uzzah brought good to Obed-edom's household. God's presence was the same in both. Obed-edom is called a Gittite, which may mean he came from the Philistine city of Gath or from a Levitical town, Gath-rimmon; whether he is the Levite of that name in chapter 15 is debated. Chapter 15 will tell the second, successful attempt.
passages.later: Second Samuel says that God struck him down ‘for his irreverence’ (2 Samuel 6:7). When Aaron's sons died at the tabernacle, Moses said, ‘To those who come near Me I will show My holiness’ (Leviticus 10:3).
passages.hard:
Why did God strike Uzzah dead when he was only trying to keep the ark from falling?

Uzzah's death has troubled readers for centuries, and David himself was angry about it. Several things are said in answer. The law was clear: the ark was to be carried on poles by Levites, and the law warned that touching the holy things meant death. The whole procession, however joyful, was done without regard for God's instructions, as David later admitted (15:13). Many interpreters also see in Uzzah's act a kind of presumption, treating the ark as an object that needed his protection, when it had been in his family's house for years and familiarity may have dulled his reverence. Others stress that this was a founding moment for Israel's worship in its new capital, and that God's judgment established from the start that he is not approached on human terms.

None of these explanations makes the story easy, and these notes do not pretend it is. The text lets David's anger and fear stand, which suggests it wants the reader to feel the weight of God's holiness rather than explain it away. The same chapter ends with good for Obed-edom's household: God's presence was not meant to destroy, but to do good to those who receive it rightly.

A word of care. This story must not be used to say that a sudden death, an accident or an illness today is God's punishment on the person who suffered it. Jesus refused that kind of reasoning: of people killed when a tower fell, he asked, “Do you think that they were more sinful than all the others living in Jerusalem? No, I tell you” (Luke 13:4-5). If you have lost someone suddenly, or carry fear or guilt after reading this, please speak with someone you trust, a pastor or a friend. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: David was angry, then afraid, and then he waited three months. Ask what you do with anger at God when you do not understand him. And ask where you have treated something holy as familiar.
